name: Liquid facelift

lead: A liquid facelift uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid, in several facial areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The change is visible immediately, giving a lifted, more youthful face.

Fillers replace volume lost with aging in facial compartments. Most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months. The phrase is a marketing term, also used in a 2018 case series for a water-jet liposuction technique alongside surgical facelift; the literature is mostly narrative reviews.

paras: A clinician plans several injection areas, such as cheeks, temples, jawline and lines around the mouth, and places filler in one session. People repeat it as the filler gradually breaks down.
Common effects are bruising, redness and pain. Rare but serious risks include infection, lumps, vascular embolization and permanent vision loss. Fillers are FDA-regulated medical devices.

angle.text: A liquid facelift is the marketing term for placing fillers, often hyaluronic acid, in several face areas in one session to restore volume and contour without surgery. The lifted look is visible immediately and lasts around six months for most fillers.

lead: 'Liquid facelift' is a marketing term for non-surgical facial rejuvenation that uses injectable fillers, often hyaluronic acid, to restore volume and contour in several areas of the face in one session. [1][2][3] The term is also used in one 2018 case series for a different technique: water jet-assisted liposuction used alongside surgical rhytidectomy. [4]

Injectable fillers are classified by the US FDA as medical devices. Wikipedia reports that most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months, and lists bruising, lumps, infection and, rarely, vision loss from vascular embolization among risks. [5]

paras: A 2010 article in Missouri Medicine describes a blending of surgical and nonsurgical techniques driven by patients' desire for an un-operated look and shorter recovery, and discusses volume loss in the facial skeleton and soft-tissue compartments, contrasting autologous fat grafting and injectable fillers with surgical rhytidectomy. [2] A 2009 nurse-practitioner article and a 2024 oral and maxillofacial surgery atlas chapter are titled 'The liquid facelift' and 'Liquid Facelift'. [3][1]

A 2018 case series of 25 patients (median age 56) in the Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive & Aesthetic Surgery reported first experience using facial water jet-assisted liposuction for facial contouring, fat harvesting and hydrodissection of the skin flap in surgical facelifts, under the heading 'liquid facelift'. [4] No randomized controlled trial of the filler-based liquid facelift was identified in the sources consulted.

Wikipedia reports that common filler effects include bruising, redness, pain and itching, less commonly infection and allergic reactions causing lumps or scarring, and rarely permanent vision loss or delayed skin necrosis from embolization. In the US only a small number of fillers are approved; in the UK and EU a CE mark certifies production standards without requiring proof of efficacy. Who may inject fillers is debated between physicians and other licensed injectors. [5]
